issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction from non-residential accommodation to use it for the landlord’s own business must establish ownership of the premises.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction of a tenant from a shop for the landlord’s own business.
The landlord claimed exclusive title under a partition deed that was not produced in court.
The property was recorded in the municipal register in the name of the landlord’s brother.
issues.conclusion: Ownership of the premises was an essential condition of the landlord’s claim under the personal-necessity ground for non-residential accommodation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, requires a landlord claiming non-residential accommodation for the landlord’s own business to be its owner; the Court reached this conclusion from the language of clause (f) and its comparison with the other clauses of section 12(1).

predicates.nonresidential_eviction_suit: A claimant brings a proceeding to evict a tenant from accommodation let for a non-residential purpose.
predicates.claimant_seeks_accommodation_for_own_bus: The claimant seeks the accommodation to continue or start the claimant’s own business.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks to evict a tenant from non-residential accommodation for the claimant’s own business, the claimant must establish ownership of the accommodation.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere in a second appeal with a factual finding when the lower appellate court’s failure to consider important evidence directly bearing on the disputed issue gives rise to a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the landlord’s claim of ownership, and the first appellate court affirmed that decision, relying in part on the absence of the partition deed.
The tenant’s reply to a pre-suit notice accepted that the shop belonged to the landlord.
Multiple rent receipts signed by the tenant described the landlord as the owner of the property.
The lower courts did not consider that evidence, while the High Court relied on it in reversing the finding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in setting aside the lower courts’ finding because their failure to consider important evidence directly bearing on ownership raised a substantial question of law.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a High Court cannot merely reappraise evidence and reverse a first appellate court’s factual finding. It may, however, interfere where the lower appellate court fails to consider important relevant evidence directly bearing on the disputed issue and the resulting error is of a magnitude that gives rise to a substantial question of law. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

predicates.second_appeal: A party brings a second appeal challenging a factual finding made by the lower appellate court.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_ignored_important_: The lower appellate court failed to consider important evidence presented by the parties.
predicates.evidence_directly_bears_on_disputed_issu: The unconsidered evidence has a direct bearing on the issue whose factual finding is challenged.
predicates.omission_raises_substantial_question_of_: The failure to consider the evidence produces an error sufficiently serious to give rise to a substantial question of law.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, if the lower appellate court ignored important evidence that directly bears on the disputed issue and that omission raises a substantial question of law, the High Court may set aside the factual finding.
